suspended.path: Something suspended is literally hung up, held in place rather than falling or moving. The sense extended to processes or rules held in place, not falling forward, put on hold.

parts.meaning: to depart, turn aside (also: to rub, scour)

swerve.path: Old English sweorfan meant both to rub or scour and to depart or turn aside; the surviving English sense narrowed to an abrupt change of direction. The link between the two old senses is unclear.

parts.meaning: to be dizzy, to act rashly

swindle.path: German Schwindler, 'a giddy or reckless person,' was borrowed into English for a reckless speculator, then narrowed to someone who dizzies others with false schemes in order to cheat them of money.

parts.meaning: ancient Greek city in Italy famed for luxury

sybarite.path: Sybaris was a Greek colony in southern Italy whose citizens were proverbial in antiquity for wealth and self-indulgence. The city's name became a byword for anyone devoted to luxury and pleasure.

sycophant.path: The literal Greek sense is disputed: possibly an informer against illegal fig exporting, or someone making a vulgar 'showing the fig' gesture. By the time it reached English it meant an informer, and later a servile flatterer who curries favor.

syllogism.path: Greek syllogismos meant a computation or inference. Aristotle used it for the formal three-part deductive argument, where a conclusion is reckoned together out of a major and minor premise.

symbiosis.path: Coined in 19th-century biology for two different organisms living together for mutual benefit, then extended to any mutually beneficial relationship, biological or not.

symmetry.path: Greek symmetria meant agreement in dimensions, parts sharing a common measure. It came to denote balanced, proportionate correspondence between parts.

synchronous.path: Direct from the parts: events that share the same time are synchronous.

syncopated.path: Syncope originally meant a cutting-short, of a word or of consciousness (a fainting fit). In music, syncopation 'cuts' the expected beat, shifting the stress to an unexpected point.

synergy.path: Greek synergos meant a fellow worker. Combined action of separate parts working together was seen to produce an effect greater than any part alone.

synoptic.path: A synoptic view takes everything in at a single glance, all parts seen together, hence a general summary rather than a detailed account.

syntax.path: Direct from the parts: syntax is how words are arranged together into sentences.

synthesize.path: Direct from the parts: to synthesize is to put separate elements together into one whole.

table.path: To 'table' a motion originally meant laying it on the board for the group to look at. British usage kept this as 'bring up for discussion'; American usage drifted to the opposite, 'set aside for later.'

tacit.path: Something tacit is agreed to or understood in silence, without being put into words.

taciturn.path: From the same root as tacit; a taciturn person habitually keeps silent rather than speaking freely.

tact.path: Tact is a figurative 'sense of touch' for social situations, an intuitive feel for the right thing to say or do around sensitive matters.

tangent.path: A geometric tangent line touches a curve at one point without crossing it. 'Going off on a tangent' borrows this image for a discussion that touches the topic briefly, then veers away.

tangential.path: Like a tangent line that meets a curve at a single point, something tangential connects to the main subject only slightly, at the margins.

tangible.path: Direct from the root: physically touchable, hence concrete and real rather than abstract.

parts.meaning: mythical king punished with unreachable fruit and water

tantalize.path: Tantalus stood in a pool beneath fruit branches that both receded whenever he reached for them. To tantalize is to tempt someone with something visible but always just out of reach.

parts.meaning: mythical king punished with unreachable fruit and water

tantalizing.path: Same myth as tantalize: something tantalizing is temptingly visible but held just out of reach.

tantamount.path: Anglo-French tant amunter meant 'to amount to so much.' Something tantamount to a thing amounts to the same as it, equal to it in effect.

tarnish.path: Originally described a bright surface, like metal, losing its shine and turning dull or dark. The figurative sense of damaging a reputation follows the same image of a lost luster.

tarry.path: The word's origin is disputed, perhaps linked to an Old English word for vexation or weariness, but the connection is unclear. Since Middle English it has simply meant to delay or linger.

tautology.path: Direct from the parts: a tautology needlessly says the same thing twice in different words.

tawdry.path: Cheap silk lace neckties sold at the fair of St. Audrey in Ely, England, were called 'St. Audrey's lace,' contracted to 'tawdry lace.' Their cheap showiness gave the word its meaning.

taxing.path: A tax is a levied burden; something taxing places a heavy demand on one's strength or resources, the way a tax strains finances.

tedious.path: Direct from the root: something tedious induces weariness through its dull length.

teem.path: Originally meant to bring forth young or produce offspring. The sense widened from a mother producing many young to any place being crowded or swarming with abundance.

telling.path: Something telling effectively 'tells' or reveals a great deal, so striking or significant in what it shows.

telltale.path: A telltale sign 'tells the tale' on its own, giving away something that was meant to stay hidden.

temerity.path: From Latin temere, 'without foresight, by blind chance,' temerity is boldness that disregards danger or propriety, confidence with no thought for the consequences.

parts.meaning: to mix in due proportion, regulate

temper.path: Originally meant combining elements in correct proportion, as in tempering metal through controlled heating and cooling. The sense extended to softening or moderating something by blending in a counteracting quality.

parts.meaning: to mix in due proportion, regulate

temperance.path: From the same family as temper: restraint achieved through balanced moderation, historically applied especially to abstaining from alcohol.

parts.meaning: to mix in due proportion, regulate

temperate.path: From the same root as temper: exercising moderation and self-restraint, or, of climate, mild and neither extreme.

parts.meaning: to mix in due proportion, regulate

tempered.path: Past participle sense of temper: qualified or balanced by an offsetting quality, as optimism tempered by caution.

tempestuous.path: A tempest is a violent storm; tempestuous extends that image to emotional or situational turbulence, as stormy and turbulent as bad weather.

temporal.path: Direct from the root: pertaining to time as opposed to eternity, and so also to worldly, secular affairs rather than spiritual ones.

temporize.literal: to act according to the time
temporize.path: To temporize is to adapt one's actions to the moment, stalling or acting evasively in order to gain time before committing to a course.

tenable.path: A tenable position is one that can be held, defended against attack or objection, literally as ground or figuratively as an argument.

tenacious.path: Direct from the root: someone tenacious holds on firmly and persistently, refusing to let go.

tenacity.path: Same root as tenacious: the quality of holding firmly to a purpose despite obstacles.

tendentious.path: A tendentious argument 'tends' or leans toward a particular conclusion, revealing an underlying bias rather than a neutral presentation of facts.

tender.path: To tender something is to hold it out or extend it formally for acceptance, as one extends a hand.

tentative.path: Something tentative is offered as a trial or test run, not yet fixed or certain.

tenuous.path: Direct from the root: stretched thin, so flimsy or barely substantial, as in a tenuous argument or connection.

tepid.path: The physical sense of merely warm, not hot, extended to reactions that are lukewarm, halfhearted, unenthusiastic.

terrestrial.path: Direct from the root: relating to the earth or land, as opposed to sea, air, or sky.
